words.definition: A healthy division of your time and energy between your job and your personal life.
words.example: Flexible working arrangements can help employees achieve a healthier work-life balance.

words.definition: The likelihood that you will be able to keep your job for a long time.
words.example: In an era of short-term contracts, job security has become something of a rarity for young graduates.

words.definition: A labour market in which people work on short-term or freelance jobs, often arranged through apps, instead of having permanent employment.
words.example: Although the gig economy offers flexibility, it often deprives workers of sick pay, holiday entitlement and pensions.
collocations: the rise of the gig economy

words.definition: The money that someone is paid for their work, including salary and other benefits.
words.example: Remuneration in the public sector often fails to reflect the value that nurses and teachers bring to society.

words.definition: A state of extreme physical and mental exhaustion caused by working too hard for too long.
words.example: A culture of long hours and constant availability inevitably leads to burnout among employees.

words.definition: The rate at which employees leave an organisation and have to be replaced.
words.example: High staff turnover is costly for companies, which must repeatedly recruit and train new employees.

words.definition: The feeling of pleasure and fulfilment that people get from their work.
words.example: Studies suggest that job satisfaction depends more on recognition and a sense of purpose than on salary alone.

words.definition: The freedom to make your own decisions about how you do something, without being controlled by others.
words.example: Giving employees greater autonomy over how they organise their tasks tends to boost both motivation and productivity.

words.definition: Doing your job from home or another place away from the employer's office.
words.example: The widespread adoption of remote working during the pandemic permanently changed attitudes towards the traditional office.

words.definition: Having lost your job because your employer no longer needs your position.
words.example: Thousands of factory workers were made redundant when production was relocated overseas.

words.definition: To learn new skills, or to train workers in new skills, so that they can do their jobs better or adapt to change.
words.example: Companies should invest in upskilling their workforce rather than simply replacing staff with machines.

words.definition: Having the qualities, such as creativity and willingness to take risks, that are needed to start new businesses.
words.example: Governments can foster an entrepreneurial culture by offering tax incentives and start-up loans to small businesses.

words.definition: An unofficial barrier that stops women or minority groups from reaching the most senior positions in an organisation.
words.example: Despite considerable progress, a glass ceiling still prevents many women from reaching board-level positions.

words.definition: A situation in which there are not enough workers available to fill the jobs that exist.
words.example: Many European countries face acute labour shortages in sectors such as social care and construction.

words.definition: Describing work that is boring, repetitive, low in status and requires little skill.
words.example: Automation may free workers from menial tasks, allowing them to focus on more creative and rewarding work.

words.definition: Something, such as money or a reward, that encourages a person to do something or work harder.
words.example: Performance-related bonuses can act as a powerful incentive, but they may also encourage unhealthy competition between colleagues.
